content: 1. It is important to express gratitude to respondents and, when appropriate, inquire if they wish to provide any additional comments. 2. A commonly employed method to assess the reliability of questionnaire results is to evaluate internal consistency, which measures the degree to which responses to different questions correlate with one another. 3. If responses are highly correlated, the test is considered internally consistent. 4. Computer programs can be designed to identify inconsistencies in responses. 5. Researchers often tend to include an excessive number of questions, a practice that has been encouraged by the advent of computer-assisted analysis. 6. In economic evaluations, the cost of an illness typically includes direct costs, such as those incurred by the healthcare system, the community, and patients’ families for diagnosis or treatment. 7. Indirect costs may be tangible or intangible. Tangible indirect costs primarily refer to productivity losses caused by the illness, borne by individuals, families, society, or employers. 8. Intangible indirect costs encompass the costs of pain, grief, suffering, and the loss of leisure time. 9. Economic evaluations estimate resources as all inputs into health service production, including time, goods, equipment, buildings, and specialized knowledge. 10. Cost-benefit analysis and cost-effectiveness analysis are related methods that compare healthcare practices or techniques based on their relative economic efficiencies in delivering health benefits. 11. Cost-effectiveness analysis compares the net monetary costs of a healthcare intervention with clinical outcomes, such as cases of disease avoided, cases identified through screening, life years gained, or deaths prevented. 12. Cost-benefit analysis compares monetary costs to the estimated monetary benefits of an intervention. 13. Cost-effectiveness analysis is often integrated into randomized controlled trials, particularly when the interventions being compared have significantly different costs or resource implications. 14. When competing interventions show minimal differences in outcomes, adding an economic perspective provides an additional dimension of evaluation. 15. Collecting prospective economic data alongside a trial allows evaluations to be based on reliable estimates of effectiveness. 16. From an ethical standpoint, health research can be categorized into four types: Research involving human experimentation, which raises the most ethical concerns. This includes therapeutic or diagnostic research on patients who may benefit from participation and purely scientific research where human subjects volunteer without expecting therapeutic or diagnostic benefits. Research involving human subjects without experimentation, such as epidemiological and field studies, which may intrude on individual or community privacy. Research involving animal experimentation, which has received increasing ethical attention. Research not involving human or animal experimentation, which must still adhere to general ethical principles. 17. All research involving human subjects must comply with the ethical principles outlined in the current version of the World Medical Association Declaration of Helsinki. 18. Researchers must adhere to principles of beneficence, non-maleficence, and respect. 19. Beneficence requires a scientifically and technically sound design, adequate sample size for valid results, and avoidance of unnecessary processes. 20. Non-maleficence requires proper evaluation and minimization of risks, adequate screening for contraindications, careful monitoring, and provision of treatment for adverse effects. 21. Respect requires fully informed and voluntary consent from participants, limited trials on children or mentally disabled individuals to conditions specific to them with parental or guardian consent, and strict confidentiality. 22. Confidentiality is an ethical obligation in medical practice and research, requiring measures to limit access to records or replace patient identifiers with codes. 23. When testing new therapies on patients, pre-clinical studies must document the potential safety of the pharmaceutical product, and manufacturing procedures must ensure suitable quality. 24. Data from previous and ongoing clinical trials should be compiled before initiating a new trial. 25. Investigators must be well-qualified, and trial sites must be adequate. 26. All parties involved in a clinical trial must comply with existing national regulations or requirements. 27. Epidemiological, field, and qualitative studies are primarily observational and generally involve no invasive interventions beyond routine medical examinations or laboratory tests. 28. While such studies carry no physical risks, they may intrude on privacy or cause psycho-social harm, which can be as significant as physical harm. 29. Ethical considerations include free informed consent, confidentiality, and beneficence. 30. Free informed consent requires that individuals understand and agree to the reasons for data collection, and communities must also consent in large surveys. 31. Confidentiality in qualitative research is based on mutual trust, and any breach of confidentiality can severely damage this trust. 32. Information collected in field studies is classified as linked or unlinked. Unlinked information cannot be associated with the individual, while linked information may still be anonymous if coded. 33. Beneficence requires informing individuals of any health conditions revealed during the study and assisting them in obtaining appropriate care. Communities have the right to be informed about study outcomes and implications. 34. Investigators have an ethical obligation to advocate for improved community health based on study results. 35. Local personnel should be utilized and trained in required skills, and ethically conducted studies should leave a positive impact on the community. 36. Research designs involving animal experimentation must use relevant animal models applicable to humans, minimize the number of animals used, and ensure scientifically valid conclusions. 37. Experiments should calculate the appropriate sample size to answer the research question or test the hypothesis, using no more than the minimum number of animals required. 38. A written protocol is essential for every research study, serving as a detailed plan that clarifies the investigators’ thoughts, guides team efforts, ensures ethical approval, and supports funding proposals. 39. Once a protocol is developed and approved, it must be strictly adhered to, especially in multi-center studies, as violations can discredit the entire study. 40. Minor protocol violations should result in the exclusion of that part of the study from analysis.
